title: Navigating Early Intervention Systems
body:
"Early intervention" generally refers to publicly funded services for infants and young children (typically birth to age 3) with developmental delays or disabilities, before they transition into preschool special education programs. Systems and exact eligibility rules vary by country and, within countries like the U.S., by state or region — but the general shape is often similar.

It usually starts with a referral or self-referral, often prompted by a pediatrician, a failed developmental screening, or a parent's own concern. This leads to an evaluation, typically free of charge, assessing areas like communication, motor skills, and social-emotional development.

If your child qualifies, you'll typically work with a coordinator to build an individualized service plan — often called an IFSP (Individualized Family Service Plan) in the U.S. — outlining specific therapies (speech, occupational, physical, developmental) delivered at a set frequency, often in your home or daycare setting rather than a clinic.

A few things help families move through this more smoothly: keep copies of every evaluation and report you receive, ask explicitly what your child does and doesn't qualify for and why, and don't wait for a formal autism diagnosis to pursue evaluation — most early intervention systems serve children with delays regardless of diagnosis.

As your child approaches the age cutoff, ask early about the transition process to preschool special education services, since eligibility criteria and paperwork requirements often differ between the two systems, and transitions can otherwise create gaps in services.
